utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, good morning to you. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. Same advisory to the accused: If at any time there are problems with interpretation, please let us know straight away. I see no differences in the presentations. Any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just one. An error in the transcript we were alerted to yesterday. It's on page 92. Several times what was translated from the witness was that he said, "Take it easy, take it easy."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I've been told by people on our team who speak the language that what he said was, "Take it slowly, slowly," on all occasions and that the translation was as, "Take it easy" but that the word really is "slowly," and that has been consistent - I think the Defence will agree - with the other times he has been here and in his statements, but I just offer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Are there any remarks from the Defence teams on this? None.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that can be corrected by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can only be corrected by referring it to the witness and having him confirm that what he said as being stated by the Serb soldier was "Take it slowly," and not "Take it easy." That's the only way we can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First we need to check whether we have the same interpreters as we had yesterday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And do you recall this part?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And would you agree with what has been suggested by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We would, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any further remarks, preliminary issues? None?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just, Your Honour, that I've reviewed the transcript and I've cut down my direct. I have no further questions of the witness, so he can proceed directly to cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Before we bring the witness in, is it still the position of the various Defence teams that each one of you would like to cross-examine this witness or are there any of you that do not feel the need for that? All right. Mr. Bourgon, do you still stand by the same -- do we still stay by the same time schedule, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's bring -- Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. One thing I should have said before I rested completely is I move to introduce now, if I need to, the exhibits from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I believe those numbers were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, let me find them so I can follow you better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Perhaps -- I've been told by Mr. McCloskey the practice in the past has also been to do it at the end of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If none of my colleagues object to that, I will have no objection. No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher. Make sure that the gallery is empty. All right. Thank you. Who is going first? Defence team for Popovic, I suppose. Let's take it in the same order as the names appear on the indictment. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back. I hope you had enough time --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- enough time to rest. Before we left this courtroom yesterday, I told you that we will have a few minutes during which Mr. Nicholls will terminate or finish his examination-in-chief. That's not going to happen. He thinks that he's finished with you already. So we are going to proceed straight away with the various cross-examinations that the various Defence teams have prepared for you. May I just remind you that yesterday you made a solemn undertaking with us that you would be testifying the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and that solemn undertaking still holds for today's sitting. You don't need to repeat it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it still holds for today's sitting. Yes. Mr. Zivanovic, who is lead counsel defending Mr. Popovic, will be the first one to go. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we go to the private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned a united vehicle -- a United Nations vehicle, a white transporter that joined the column somewhere around Vidikovac. You did not see that, did you, but you heard of that. Would you please answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I did not see it when the people who were on the lorry who said that they saw the lorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They saw the transporter during the column.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I saw it in Orahovac in the courtyard of the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And I'll have just one more question. The soldiers who were on that transporter, you saw them only in the courtyard of the school in Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, only in Orahovac, nowhere else. They wore UNPROFOR uniforms, but on the APC there were no UNPROFOR markings. The only thing I saw was a letter C, which is an S in the Latinic. The soldiers did not react. The civilians did not -- the civilian did not react. Those were Serb soldiers who had captured an APC, or maybe even more APCs, and they pretended to be UNPROFOR troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no more questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Zivanovic. Is it Mr. Meek who is going next?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Meek is representing Accused Beara. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May I get the podium, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Well, so-so. As you see me sitting here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, you just testified that you concluded that these two individuals with UN uniforms were imposters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a hundred per cent. I'm a hundred per cent positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... sir, that you testified yesterday under oath that you just watched them and that they had no reaction whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I am testifying under oath, but you also have to tell the truth, because all those who lie has to go there and sit with those who did whatever they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment. Look at me, Witness. Witness. Witness. Look at me, please. Mr. Meek, like Mr. Nicholls, like Mr. Popovic, like every other lawyer in this courtroom, is here to do his -- perform his duty towards his respective client. It's a basic principle of law that Mr. Meek has a right to put questions to you on behalf of his client, and you have taken an undertaking with us that you will not make any distinction between Prosecution and Defence when it comes to answering questions, because wherever the questions are coming from, you are going - that's what you promised us - to give us a straight, clean answer which is the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Last thing I want from you is to enter into a confrontation with any of the lawyers. If you don't agree with what is being put to you, you have every right to say, "I don't agree," but you have no right to speak to Mr. Meek or to any other representative of the various accused in the way you did, and certainly not to make allegations that Mr. Meek is trying to put false things to you is or not speaking the truth. Have I made myself clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very clear, Mr. President. I am only trying to tell him that those who wore uniforms, UNPROFOR uniforms, they did not react in any way. None of the soldiers did not come and ask us anything. Don't put words into my mouth. I survived all this, and there is no money that would make me testify falsely against anybody. I'm telling the truth, like I said I would. And if these people are not guilty, just put them on a plane and send them back home, because my tragedy cannot be paid by anything or anybody. Please, let's not deceive ourselves. I am going to answer his questions, but there's nobody who can convince me that things were not the way I saw them. I am just telling you the truth. Let everybody see that I was not ill-treated. I'm not going to tell you what is not the truth. I have a heart. I am a parent. I'm a human being, and not even Toma Fila, if they brought Toma Fila from Belgrade, he would not prove me wrong. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, I can help calm things down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I ask for a recess for this witness to calm him down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think there is a need for one. I think I will calm him down. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you know, this witness has testified many times before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Actually, three times in -- and he has done -- he has done well. He has -- he has strong, strident views, but he has done well. This is the fourth time. I think he's having a harder time because of that, and I think he will understand that he needs to stay calm and that he does feel strongly that they're just doing their job, and I wanted to communicate that to you and to him, for everyone, so he can do the job that he did last time and just do his best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I am sure -- I'm going to address you instead of him, but I am sure that he's all ears and that he will understand exactly what I am going to say. He needs to understand that when a Defence counsel stands up and tries and insists with him that something was white and not black, the fact that there is this insistence on the part of the -- of Defence counsel does not mean that he is being forced to agree. If he doesn't agree, he just has to say, "Counsel, you're wrong. I don't accept this. It was black and not white. It was white and not black." All he has to do is to respect the role and the function of each one of the Defence counsel here. It could also happen to you later on when you get these witnesses that you have anticipated would not be exactly confirming what you would like them to confirm, but the thing is that he's here to answer questions. With every question that there is that he doesn't agree with what is being suggested to him, he simply has to say, "I don't agree. No, you're wrong, Mr. Meek." He doesn't have to argue with Mr. Meek. He is not here to argue with anybody. He's just here to answer the questions that are put to him. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are trying to help you out, and I am sure, because I've been watching you for a whole day testifying, that you are a very clever, intelligent man, and I am sure that you have understood me. So please, cool it, calm down. And when Mr. Meek or whoever it will be that will follow him that will put questions that you find irritating, just answer the question and forget the irritation. I know that you have passed through a hell of a lot, but this is why you are here. And once you have accepted to come here and give testimony, you have to subject yourself to all the questions that are put to you. Provided that they are legitimate questions which we will allow, then you have to answer them. The moment there is a question which should not be put to you, we will stop it and then you will not be required to answer it. But until we say so, you will need to answer all the questions that are put to you in a calm manner, without entering into a direct confrontation, collision, with any of the Defence counsel who are here to do their job. Agreed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And I thank you so much for understanding and also for your cooperation. And if we continue like that, you will soon be on your way back home. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, first I would like to tell you that I understand that you went through, like the Judge said, a hell of a lot, and I appreciate you coming here to testify. Thank you. That's not a question. And I will try to phrase my questions -- sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't understand. I apologise. You don't understand. If you did understand, you would never ask me wrong questions, although you may have right to put them to me. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Mr. Meek, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: As the Judge said, if you don't agree with something I say, just tell me, "I don't agree." My wife tells me I'm wrong all the time, and it's okay if you do too; all right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all make mistakes. We all make mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, I'll try to phrase my questions where you can answer in a yes or a no. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: These two UN personnel that were dressed and by the UN vehicle, you never spoke to them, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell me roughly how many metres away from you these two UN soldiers were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were at the entrance to the courtyard. They were just walking there. They'd never approached us. They were the soldiers who ordered us to run into the school as we got off the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. So when you testified yesterday that they -- they reacted in no way whatsoever --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- are you now today saying they did react in some way and they're the ones who told you to run into the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So, not to belabour this, you never spoke to them; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not speak to any soldier whatsoever, not only to those two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And they had an interpreter with them; correct? That's what you testified to yesterday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a man in his 50s with somewhat greyish hair; a big man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, can you tell me, Mr. Witness, approximately how many statements have you given to the investigators for this International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can't remember. For this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this here? For this here? Four times. I've testified four times, with the testimony today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And as far as sitting down and giving written statements or statements which you read and then signed, do you remember how many times you have done that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: God only knows. I've never counted those. I have given a number of statements in Bosnia, and I have not given any statements here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, do you recall speaking to the investigators on the 13th and 14th of August in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 13 and 14 I don't remember. I never carried those papers on me. If you have them and if that is what it says, then that's correct. If you don't have those papers, then I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will simplify it for you, Witness, because I don't think it's fair to put 13th and 14th of August, 1995, just like that. 13th, 14th of August is just one month after the events in Srebrenica. Did you ever give a statement to an investigator just one month after the events in Srebrenica in 1995 or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I gave my first statement in the District Court in Tuzla, to a lady called Ajsa Kapic, and I don't know when that was. I can't remember any of the dates. That was a long time ago. That was 11 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, on the 11th of July, 1995, you and your brother and other people decided to leave Srebrenica and go to Tuzla; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And didn't you in fact go to a rally that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What rally, where?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: A meeting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A meeting. No. No. On the 11th of July, everybody left Srebrenica; the women, the children, the able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But before you left, and I believe because you've testified in three previous trials here, that you went to a meeting with your brother before you left to go to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. We never -- never had any meetings about the departure. We didn't know that that would happen. We just knew that the situation around Srebrenica had gotten worse, but we didn't know what would happen. We were absolutely sure that any zone under the United Nations protection could ever fall, because that would have been worse than for any other town which was -- was in a protected area to fall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek, what, may I ask you, is the relevance of this line of questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Judge, if it please the Court, the witness has testified previously there was a rally which he and his brother attended on the 11th, and there was a decision made at that time that they should leave, a lot of folks. Not just he and his brother, but many people from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, what's the relevance of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The relevance is I would like to know from this witness who are the leaders, because he's testified previously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall, Witness, testifying in the Krstic case, General Krstic -- his trial, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It may have been the case that on that day people met to talk about what was going on and to discuss this, but I didn't go there. On that day I was simply thinking hard about what to do. That was all before the order came that we had to leave because UNPROFOR could not settle things. Shells started falling. Whoever didn't witness this wouldn't be able to tell you this. I saw women and children go to the UN base at Vidikovac, and the women, once they saw a truck parked there, although there was no driver, they were trying so hard to get on the truck that they tore apart the tarpaulin that was up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you just testified that: "That was all before the order came that we had to leave because UNPROFOR could not settle things." You just stated that. Now, my question to you is who gave the order?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To whom? To us? Well, we took the decision ourselves. There was no one else. You know what happened to the elderly people at Potocari. Gentlemen, what would have become of us? We would have been shot like dogs. Please, come. Those were elderly people aged 80 or 90 who were killed. What was there else for us to do? Even the children were taken away. I am here just to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek. I think he has answered your question. If you insist on this subject and would like to suggest to him specific names, go ahead, but otherwise drop it and move to the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'll just ask the witness this question:

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Where was the meeting that you -- where did it take place before the order came for you to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been held in the area of Srebrenica, perhaps near Vidikovac. I wasn't there, so this may not have been the case, but it was on that day that Srebrenica fell, and there's nothing else for me to say. You know, you gentlemen, Serbs, you know what you did. Please try and save your soul. We will all die, and there there will be no lawyers, I tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you continue like this, I will have to stop you and send you home --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And send you home. And you would have come here in vain. You would have wasted your time and our time. I don't think you have understood -- let me finish, please. I don't think you have understood. I said answer the question and stop sending accusations here and there to anyone. You're here to answer the questions that are put to you, and please stick to that. Otherwise, I will conclude your -- your testimony here and send you home, and you would have wasted two precious days for us. Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, I've read your statements, all six of them that I have in my possession, and I've read your testimony from your other three events when you testified in this Tribunal. Who made -- your wife and children had already left to go to Potocari, correct, on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My wife and my children were never at Potocari. My wife and my children were at Tuzla, in the municipality of Srebrenica, in the Tuzla canton. I never stated that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And when did they leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My family --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. Answer the question, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My family left on the 30th of January or the 1st of February, 1993, on foot for the free territory of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you testified yesterday that you believe there to be 15 to 20.000 Muslims in the column that was heading towards Tuzla; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell me how it is that you arrived at this estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The estimate was based on the line-up, the observation of the people who were seated in the meadow. This was simply an estimate. Of course, the figure could go up or down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And when you just mentioned meadow, which meadow are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meadow at Susnjari and during the journey toward Susnjari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And you testified that it was a very long column; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And can you tell me, approximately how long was that column; one kilometre, two kilometres, three kilometres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could estimate it at 10 kilometres, perhaps more, judging by how many people were walking, because the lay of the terrain was such that it hardly permitted the civilians to walk in twos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And the terrain did not permit you to see the entire column; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no one was able to see it entirely ever, because we know that the column was cut off, and I was toward the rear of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And in the part of the column, the portion of the column that you could see, you've estimated that there were at least 4 to 500 armed Muslim soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The ones who were armed left with the first columns. In the last columns, there were hardly any armed people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again, am I correct in stating that it's your estimate that 4 to 500 of the individuals, Muslim soldiers, in that column were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The ones who were around left first. The ones who were left behind unarmed, one knows what their fate was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And yesterday, you testified that it was very difficult to tell how many people were armed. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, of course it's quite natural that you can't count the weapons when there's so many people around. That's only natural. But it was just an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And that -- you would agree with me, Witness, that estimate could have been very low and there could have been 5.000 armed troops in that column; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had there been 5.000 armed troops, things would never happen the way -- would have never happened the way they did. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, in July -- excuse me, in June - specifically on the 13th of June, 1999 - Investigator Ruez from this Tribunal, from the Office of the Prosecutor, met with you in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did he not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. He met with me, but I think he also met with me in 1995, just as he did in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell me, what was the purpose of your meeting on June 13th of 1999 when you went to the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of it was to go to the spot where we were executed, to see the spot where we were taken prisoner. That was the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And did you accomplish that purpose, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And during that excursion, did you show Investigator Ruez exactly where the location -- you believe the location of the field where the killings took place was located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did show him for the meadow where I was, but as for the other meadow, I wasn't sure about it. I know that the fields were near to each other, but I was 100 per cent positive about the meadow where I was, where I stood.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that Investigator Ruez did not have to take you to a field and ask you, "Is this the location?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He -- or, rather, based on my statement, the site was found right away and was secured with barbed wire. The cornfield that I mentioned, in that particular field corn had not been -- had not ever been reaped, cut, so basically the same cornstalks that were there at the time I was there still stood at that later visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, previous -- previously, you had in fact sat down with investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor, and they showed you a series of pictures, did they not, and a video that was filmed by Peter Nicholson? Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I watched it, then I must remember it. Well, if I didn't, then of course I would not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And after you looked at that video and after you looked at the pictures, you told the Office of the Prosecutor that the area shown on the film might be the zone of the execution but that you did not recognise anything on that film. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: As far as the diagrams are concerned, or film, it's always impossible for me to recognise the spot on the basis of this. I am not a construction -- a civil engineer to be able to read into any sort of drawings. I can only describe it for you and then it's up to you to go down into the field to the location. I cannot be asked to talk about these things on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So you didn't recognise anything in the video, and you told the investigators that; correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm telling you, as far as the video clip is concerned -- well, you see, yesterday when I was showing the hall, and I was trying to point to a wall, but the picture seemed to be like a photocopy and wasn't clearly visible as it would have been if I were there. I can describe the area for you. On the basis of my statement that I gave in 1995, they immediately drew their conclusions, because I myself was blindfolded. I was in a lorry. But when I was brought -- when I was brought there, I couldn't get my bearings, but when I was running away, when I came across the railway, I tried to make my conclusions. When I was being taken there, I was in a lorry that was covered in. It was just on the basis of these other indications like the underpass that I saw, or a flyover that was there, and it was on the basis of these indications that I was able to get my bearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, in all your discussions with Investigator Ruez from the Office of the Prosecutor, did he ever indicate to you that the number of people in this column was approximately 15 to 20.000 people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who, Ruez?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Ruez, yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that. Ruez could not have said that. He wasn't there with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. On the day that you decided to surrender when you were in the hills and the Serb soldiers were on megaphones, you've testified that you surrendered about 3.00 in the afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In the afternoon. They gave us an ultimatum. It -- it may have been gone 3.00, but the ultimatum was for 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And tell me again what day that was, sir, if you recall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Later that afternoon, you've testified that a gentleman came and it was, to your knowledge, General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. And how long had you been in that meadow before General Mladic appeared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We must have been there for some three to four hours. I can't tell you precisely because I didn't have a watch. And Mladic came just before dusk. It wasn't dark yet. And he greeted us by saying, "Good evening, Neighbours."

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. You previously testified that he arrived approximately an hour to an hour and a half before nightfall. Does that refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was close to nightfall, but the sun was still there. After Mladic left, when we were on our way from that spot to Bratunac, dark had -- darkness had already set in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Could we have page and dates and where these previous testimonies are coming from so that I can follow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're perfectly right --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I was going to do that, Judge. It's on page 2658, the Krstic trial, starting at line 20 through 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, if your family left in 1993 and you remained till 1995, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a farmer. I -- I was helping people who had their farms and who were still there. So I was trying to help them farm their fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that you've never been a member of any armed services or armed forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was not in Srebrenica. I was -- before Srebrenica I was with the Territorial Defence. We did not have an army. Bosnia-Herzegovina was attacked as a country without an army. Tuzla formed corps, and I don't know when it was, but we didn't have that. We had the Territorial Defence and whatever means we had at our disposal to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could you tell me what year or years you were a member of the Territorial Defence, and which location, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in my hometown when my hometown was attacked. We were defending ourselves. And then when Srebrenica fell, I was also a member of the army, because they wanted to relieve me of my military duty after the tragedy I went through. However, I didn't want to. And then came the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment, because we need to be very specific. Srebrenica fell twice. It fell in 1992, and it fell again in 1995. In 1992, it was taken by the Bosnian Muslims. So let's take it from the beginning of the war in April, 1992. You said you were in a territorial fighting group in your hometown. Is that Kamenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I wasn't at Srebrenica. It was on the 14th of March, 1993, that I arrived in Srebrenica, not before ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You told us that yesterday. So you were in the territorial force in Kamenica from what time to what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime between end of April and 1993 when we left Kamenica. I was a member, but as I said, we never had an army. We were able to help one another, and there were quite a few of us, but the area was large and maybe there were 100 armed people for every 1.000 citizens. We surrendered our weapons to Serbs, and the receipt was signed by A. Cecalic. I think he was a warrant officer. I'm sure the Serbs would know who he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And then when you said that you again took up arms again after Srebrenica fell, you're referring to post-July, 1995, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That was at the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. It's clear. Thank you. Mr. Meek, I am not going to stop you, of course, but you started your cross-examination at 9.13. You knock off five minutes that we have spent on other matters, you're approaching -- or you are approaching three-quarters of an hour. So I'm not going to stop you, but of course there are other Defence teams that have indicated -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I appreciate that and I hope Your Honours can appreciate that all the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Did you ever serve, sir, in the JNA army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm -- I served my service for the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And when did you serve in the JNA, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And for how long did you serve in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For 15 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And where were you based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether I should state that since I'm a protected witness. Perhaps I should consult the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it important for you to know, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. May we go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are back in open session. Thank you, Mr. Meek, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, I only have a few more questions. The first one is why did you not go to the free territory with your family when they left previous to -- prior to July 11, 1995, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you why I didn't want to leave: Because if I leave and my family leaves and we get captured, then all of us would perish. And there's another thing. I'm a parent. I have two daughters and one son. The hardest blow to me would be to see my daughter raped by someone. That's the most difficult thing that can happen to a person. That would be even worse for me than to have my daughter killed by a Chetnik and have to bury her. That's the sort of person I am. I think that's the worst humiliation a person can experience. And this was something that was happening in the neighbouring village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm from Kansas in America, and you just used the term "Chetnik." Is that a derogatory term, sir, or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And do you know why? Because they themselves behaved that way, you know. And I told you yesterday, when people addressed them by soldiers, they said, "No, we're not soldiers. We are Karadzic's Chetniks, Young Karadzic's Chetniks." So they prided themselves on that. So we may be interacting in this way, but they do pride themselves on that fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you tell me, describe, what is a Chetnik? What is that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do we have to belabour this, Mr. Meek? Don't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: One other question, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer the question. Move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I understand why you've now told me that you did not go with your family to the free territory. My next question is: At some point you knew they were in the free territory and they were safe. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know when I knew? As a group crossed over, they would let us know so many had come, and we didn't know who these people were. In 1993, in April, May, June or July, the Red Cross registered our families. They were taken to a place and then the lists of their names had arrived, and it is only then when I realised that they had crossed safely. For two or three months I didn't know their whereabouts. I only knew that some groups did manage to save themselves, but I didn't know whether my family was among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I take it, then, that around April, May, June or July of 1993, you did become aware, though, that they were registered with the Red Cross and were safe in the free territory; correct? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. My next question is: Why didn't you go to the free territory after you knew that your family was safe? Why did you stay in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where should I leave from? Should I have left to lose an arm, a leg, or my life? I was 40-something. What did you expect me to do, to walk barefoot through the Serb lines? How would I have managed to cross through? I would have liked to live with my family. It is only now that I'm a happy man, that I am living with my family. Gentlemen, I spent all my life working in the field; in Belgrade, all over the place. I worked long hours. I held jobs in order to build my house, and that was all destroyed within the scope of one day. I lost everything. When I finally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, I said stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- arrived somewhere, it was with one little bag in my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It was a simple question which required just one sentence. Yes, Mr. Meek, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, in the last few days or weeks since you've been in The Hague to testify in this courtroom, have you met with any other witnesses who are going to be testifying in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now Mr. Bourgon, who is appearing for Mr. Nikolic, will be putting some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know it's very early, but maybe it would be good to have a short break now before the next segment of the cross, just for the witness to relax for about 15 or 20 minutes. It's just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay with you, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have absolutely nothing against that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 20-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With your permission, I'd like to move immediately into private session for a quick question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, I will proceed with my cross-examination and ask you a few questions, as I mentioned, to clarify a few issues. The first one I would like to clarify with you is the -- the time when, of course, you decided, along with other people, to depart from Srebrenica and head for the free territory. Do you recall that time when you decided to leave Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, when you -- as you were going towards the free territory, there came a time when you decided, along with another group of individuals, to surrender to Serb soldiers. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And if I understood you correctly, it was a tough decision to surrender, and also a very stressful event, and it took some time before you actually decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They gave us ultimatums. The first time was until 10.00, and then we couldn't agree. We just shouted aloud. Then this ultimatum was moved to 1500 hours, and after that we decided to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, when you did decide to surrender, I've got information from one of your conversations with one of the investigators that said you were at that time so stressed that you would -- you were not in any position to identify any military insignia. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. When we finally decided to surrender, there were no military insignia. When we arrived at the place where we finally surrendered, there were military insignia there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, when you met this man who you identified as being Mladic, who addressed your group a little later, I would just like you to confirm with me that after he had spoken to you, you were satisfied as to what was going to happen. You thought you were going to be exchanged, and you actually applauded Mr. Mladic before he left.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He encouraged us by his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, sir, I will move immediately to the time that you arrived in Orahovac. And I take it from your testimony and the material that I have that you were able to know that you arrived in Orahovac sometime around noon, and you knew this because of the position of the sun; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I think we may have arrived sometime in the afternoon. Judging by the time we spent sitting there when people started leaving, I left before sunset. I suppose we arrived sometime during the evening, because summer days are very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, if there are references to testimony, I'd like to know when we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct. Will you be dwelling on this any further?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, I will, and I am simply -- just because of the answer, be quoting the exact reference. And I need to go into -- let me see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's adopt a practice, Mr. Bourgon, and all the other Defence teams, that when you are specifically referring the witness to any previous testimony or prior statements, out-of-court statements, that you make it clear what you're referring to, and if there is going to be a series of questions, that the copy of the statement is made available, handed to the witness so he can actually follow what was being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Although I understand that most -- most of the time it would be in English and he wouldn't understand it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I fully agree, Mr. President. I just thought this was a non-contested issue, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- I will find a reference because I don't have it with me now. The reference I have is not the right one, but I will move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, sir, after you arrived in Orahovac, you mentioned that there were 30 vehicles, or abouts thereof, in the convoy leading to Orahovac. Now, I suggest to you that you were not in a position to tell us whether all of these vehicles made it to Orahovac or whether some of those might have gone to another location.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I am telling you that I don't know whether all the vehicles made it to Orahovac. I just saw the convoy towards Glogova. There is Avdaga's field, and from there I could see the convoy. Mind you, nobody dared lift their head above the sides of the lorry. Only those who were in the buses might have seen the whole column. And you are right, I'm not in a position to know whether the entire convoy made it to Orahovac or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you yourself mentioned that you were in -- to the best of your knowledge, in the rear of that column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm sorry, I don't think that question's very clear. He's talking about convoys and columns, which are different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would appreciate that if my colleague is going to interrupt my cross-examination he should wait until the witness has a problem answering my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, please. Calm, calm down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- without there being a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Nicholls, please calm down. The question was: "Now, you mention yourself that you were in -- to the best of your knowledge, in the rear of that column ..." That's what we have in the transcript. So there is no confusion there between a convoy or a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- at least -- I'm not talking to you for the time being, sir. I'm just conversing with Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Nicholls. So let's not make a storm in a teacup on this issue. But again, we will control when objections are to be heard and at what time. And when you stand up, Mr. Nicholls - and that applies again to any of the Defence teams - wait until we give you the go-ahead. I mean, you know what some of the tactics are, and it's important that especially the witness is allowed to start and finish his statement without any suggestions, without any interruptions, unless we give the go-ahead. Question, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, I will simply try to say that it is my understanding from your testimony yesterday that amongst those vehicles going to Orahovac, you were not in the first vehicle, you were more towards the end of that column going towards Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not either towards the rear or in the front. I was in the middle. When we left Susnjari on foot, I was amongst the last to leave. I was at the rear of that column of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, when you -- I move into the time when you are moving into the sports hall. You mentioned yesterday that as you come in the sports hall is half full and that people coming -- continue to come in after you for about five or six minutes. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I'd also like to confirm with you that in the sports hall you saw four young people sitting by themselves in a separated area of the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not young people, they were children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: But my point, sir, is that they were sitting by their own -- on their own in a different part of the gym.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were to a far end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, I would just like to clarify with you that the time you arrive in the sports hall and the time for the first group of people to leave on the TAM truck, that this includes several hours. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. As the column started leaving, it went interruptedly -- without any interruptions. Only for a while people started slowing down and pushing as if they were getting on a bus, but then when they -- when they slowed down, then the soldiers started shouting at them, "You all have to pass through here." And then when I left, from then on I don't know how the others left after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, sir, probably this was my mistake because my question was not clear enough. What I'm trying to clarify from you is that you entered the sports hall at a certain time, and then the -- some people from the sports hall started to leave to be taken on TAM trucks. So that you were in the sports hall for a long period of time before the first group left on the TAM trucks. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We all spent a certain time there. Then the command was issued by the soldier in the red beret, and as from then our eyes were blindfolded and we started leaving. And all of us had spent a few hours there at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'll go on to the events while you are sitting in this sports hall, because you referred in your testimony to some events, and my sole purpose now is just to place these events in order. Now, my understanding is that the first event that took place is when some officers or people you considered to be officers walked into the sports hall. That's the first major event that took place. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When we were to be taken away, a group of soldiers came. Maybe they were officers, but they didn't have caps on their heads or insignia on their pockets. I did not see any of those. Then they issued a command for the four rows of people from Potocari to stand up and turned towards the right. Usually that command is to turn towards the left. And they had to turn their faces towards the wall and backs towards the door. And then this continued down to the middle of the hall, and from then on it was the other way round; our faces were turned to the door and our backs were turned to the wall. And maybe 10 or 15 minutes later the first men were blindfolded and started being taken away through that door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. That's what I -- I wanted to establish that the first people to be blindfolded, and when the blindfolds were brought into the sports hall, that was after these officers showed up. Please answer by yes or no if you agree.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the blindfolds. Maybe the blindfolds had been used even before the officers came. In any case, the blindfolds were held by that woman that I mentioned and the two men, two officers, two soldiers, who were in that adjacent room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now -- you referred yesterday in your testimony to an incident where a man was taken out of the sports hall because he had made a comment that these people should not be killed. Do you remember making this in your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When all of us were lined up, this man was on the right-hand side in the upper part of the sports hall, and when we were all lined up, the people who had arrived left, those people who had lined us up, and then this man, the captured man, said, "These people should not be killed." I only know that he had black trousers on and a white shirt. And then a Serb soldier who was standing at the door asked, "Who says that?" And then this man repeated his words, "These people should not be killed." And the soldier was a short man, around 25 or 30 years of age. He was not either young or old. And then he said, "Okay. Let's see if they should or they shouldn't. You come first." And then this man was taken out. There was a rifle shot, the person screamed, there was another shot, and the man was quiet. Another person was taken out from the school building. Again there was a rifle shot, and the person could not be heard and he wasn't returned. In the meantime, those people who were also detainees and who brought us water were prevented from -- for some time to bring any more water. I don't know why they did that. Maybe they wanted to cover up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. You just have to say yes or no. You didn't have to repeat the whole story over again. You've already told us this. If you continue like this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If need be, I'll repeat it all again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will not repeat it all again unless you're asked to repeat. Otherwise, just answer the question and only the question. And if the question just solicits a yes or no answer, please restrict yourself to that, because otherwise you'll be here the whole day and again on Monday and again on Tuesday and you'll never finish with your testimony. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, sir, I did not want to interrupt you because -- if I can avoid doing that I will always do so, but the question was simply: Did this take place after the men who you considered to be officers arrived? And I guess you'll agree with me the answer to this question is yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said it. Yes. That's the first word of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I only wanted to repeat what I said yesterday. Maybe tonight, when I'm asleep in my bed in the hotel, at midnight somebody should come and wake me up and I will repeat it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, the next question is that I would just like to go again over with you simply the sequence of events. That's all I'm trying to get at. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And first there was those officers that came into the sports hall. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Then there was the event where a man was taken outside because he had made a comment about he did not want those people to be killed. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And then there was the event of being blindfolded and bringing the blindfolds into the gym. That's after the officers, or those you considered to be officers, arrived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I suppose things are done on orders. Nothing is done without an order having been issued, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And just one more question concerning those events into the sports hall: The man with the red beret, you can confirm that this man was kind of running the situation in the sense that he was taking the people outside of the sports hall. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When he arrived, he took people from the sports hall to the execution. Before he came, nobody was taken out. I'm not saying that I am a hundred per cent sure that he was the boss of all that, that he was running the situation, but he was the one who took people from the sports hall to the execution site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, you mentioned when I -- when we look at the events as you described them, would you agree that there was a change in the atmosphere in the sports hall after those you considered to be officers arrived in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They issued commands. They asked us to be quiet. It was very hot. It was noisy. People were crammed into the room. They ordered us to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- be quiet and they realigned us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I just wanted to know whether there was a change after these officers came into the gym. Now, I'll move on to the next --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- to my next question. It is: You mentioned that the guards who were there shot some -- fired some shots in the windows for the people to be quiet. Do you remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's a slight misstatement. I think he said shots into the walls, is what I remember. I don't have a transcript with us, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we need to check that, we can check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I do remember definitely the shots at the walls, and he said you can still see them. That's my recollection. Or, rather, that they were still there when he went on the -- but that's what I recall, but I can't rule out that he also mentioned windows. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Whether it's windows or walls, I'm just going to ask the witness whether he remembers saying that there were shots fired to keep people quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Do you recall this, Mr. -- sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, sir, most people in this courtroom would not know this, but if you fire a shot into a sports hall, would you agree with me that this makes an incredible sound that actually can make you lose your hearing for some minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me rephrase the question for Mr. Bourgon. Did you go through this experience when these shots were fired? In other words, do you -- do you believe now with hindsight that there was this incredible sound and that actually made you lose your hearing for some minutes? Did you go through this experience or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. The noise was really great, however, no, we didn't -- I didn't experience that. I could only see that at that later visit there were still traces of the bullets that were fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I rephrased it, Mr. Bourgon, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- the witness is not an expert. He can only tell you what his experience was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, my question is not whether you lost your hearing. My question is does a bullet fired into a sports hall, when you were there, does it make an incredible sound? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered that question. He said that makes a hell of a lot of sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, I will now move on to in terms of -- yesterday you mentioned that -- and I would like you to confirm that you did not count the number of persons in the sports hall. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And I would like you to confirm also that when you were in Orahovac, you did not see any military police or civilian police there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As we were entering the perimeter, there olive-grey uniforms and camouflage uniforms. Now, whether the military and the police had different uniforms, that's something I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I have here an information report of an information that was discussed between you and an investigator from the Tribunal where the investigator -- now, I refer to an information report for my colleague dated the 26th of January, 1998. And it says in here that the witness saw no civilian or military police, and he knows that military police wear white belts. Is that correct information, sir, that you know that military police wear white belts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yes. That's what they used to wear before. I don't know what they wore in wartime. I know that in peacetime the military police wore white belts. However, this was no longer the JNA. It was a new army. We didn't know what the insignia of your army was. I could only read on the left-arm sleeve the Army of Republika Srpska. That's where we were taken prisoners. Now, as for these young men there where we were all sitting, there were so many people and they were further away from me, I wasn't able to make out what they had if they had anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, sir, I suggest to you that if they had been wearing a white belt, you would have seen that at the time, would you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm saying that for a fact there was no military police there. I only don't know whether there was any civilian police there, because they normally had blue uniforms or camouflage uniforms. Now, there were different uniforms there. I know that when we were part of the JNA that we had these sort of uniforms. Now, this particular army had different types of uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll move on to my next question, which is -- relates to the time that you are taken to a site where the execution takes place, and my question is simply that I would like to know when, after the execution took place - I mean after people were shot - you were lying down on the ground but still alive. Now, it's my understanding that this must have been the most terrible experience in your life. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you heard a conversation at that time which was taking place close to an excavator, which was about 10 metres from you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The distance may have been more than 10 metres, but it was thereabouts. There was the excavator working, I was lying down with my blindfold. I dared not to move. I don't know whether there was -- I didn't know who was next to me. Only when it became dark and as my body went numb did I decide to move. I had a large bloodstain on my shirt from the body that was lying over me, and I had this wound that was probably inflicted by a stone, because the wound wasn't that severe. I can even show it to you. I, of course, have to have glasses to see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, this machine that we are talking about, the excavator, which could have been more than 10 metres away from you, it had -- the engine was running. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The engine was running, working normally, digging up and throwing up earth, and the rear part of the machine was facing us. So the headlights were facing in the other direction. It was only later on when another -- when another excavator came that the lights went over the bodies, including myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we move in private session for a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I indicated to the Court, sir, that I had 30 minutes for my cross-examination, so I only have a few more questions for you which relate to the time that you escaped from this site. And I have information in the same statement here that when you got up, your T-shirt was soaked with blood. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the entire T-shirt. It was just a round stain on my back. I don't know. It must have been the blood flowing from the bodies around me, beneath me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Sir, I will simply quote you from what you -- information you gave to the investigators in the same statement. That's 13th and 14th August - and for my colleagues, I quote page 6 in English version of that statement - where it says: "Later, after I escaped, I discovered that the lower back of my T-shirt was soaked with blood." Do you recall this, or is this -- can this correspond to the reality as you lived it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There was this round stain on the small of my back. And if I had it here, I'd show it to you now, because people asked me to provide them with the T-shirt for identification purposes. And actually, I didn't carry any of my belongings, so that was the only thing that I had on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll simply move on to asking you to confirm that when you did run away -- and you explained that yesterday, so there's no need to go back again into how you ran away, but I just want you to confirm that there were shots fired and that people tried -- they were looking for you when you tried to escape, but they did not find you, and the shots did not hurt you, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They went round the cornfield, and I was in the cornfield. It was a ditch, and I could hear the sound of water. I didn't see it. And they were firing shots without entering the cornfields. I don't know where they were shooting or what they were shooting at. I could only hear tree branches breaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I'd just like to discuss briefly with you the -- an event which took place the following morning when you met a Serb soldier. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-110 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I reached the free territory, but I was terribly frightened because I thought that I had come across a Serb soldier. I think that was the following day. And I ran away from the man because I was 100 per cent sure that this was a Serb soldier because it was close to the area where the people managed to break through. The man offered me a cigarette, and I introduced myself to him, but he introduced himself to me in a wrong way, and I thought he was a Serb soldier. So I went back into the Serb territory. I wandered there and went back to the place I initially ran away from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... problem with the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. The witness mentioned Baljkovica and it is not entered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In what context did he actually mention it? As being the place where he was or -- "I reached the free territory. I was terribly frightened because I had come across a Serb soldier. I think that was close to the area where the people managed to break through." Is it there that he mentioned it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Line 17.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel, come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Line 17. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Line 17, it's still Mr. Bourgon, actually, but -- Witness, did you at any time mention the place Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Baljkovica and the free territory were adjoining territories. I had this misunderstanding with this soldier. I was terribly frightened, and I thought he was a Serb soldier, and I ran away from him. And this man told my nephew, "Ask this man whether I had offered him a cigarette," and indeed I was a smoker at the time, and he did offer me a cigarette. But he, perhaps thinking that I might be a Serb soldier, acted strangely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. At this time I would simply like to show part of statement which was given by the witness. So I'll try the e-court technology for the first time. And so I would like to refer and ask the court usher to show document 3D -- Yes, 3D1. And that is on -- 3D1, and that is page 7. Sorry, page 8. Can we have this on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before we do that, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The statement, I don't know how it's going to come up, but the statement has the witness's signature on the bottom of each page. So if we show the statement, we have to make sure the signature is not shown.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and do that in private session, than will solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I have one last question for you, Witness, and that is simply that we can understand from your testimony that you were taken to an execution site, but you were lucky enough not to be injured. You escaped from that execution site, and you were not injured. And you escaped from further soldiers and you're still not injured for a third time. Is that correct?
